Unit A: Polygons & Angles
CS 6.1 · 6.2
1

Blueprints in Orbit

🎨Zara & Ken at the design console, glowing polygons floating in the cabin
images/c6_a1_design.jpeg

High above the rainforests of Sarawak, Zara and Ken floated inside Stesen Hornbill, Malaysia’s first space station. Today’s job: design the station’s new modules.

Zara tapped her console and glowing shapes lit up the cabin. “Every part of a space station starts as a shape!”

A regular polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal, such as a triangle (3 sides), a square (4), a pentagon (5), a hexagon (6). Ken counted a hexagon window: 6 straight sides, 6 corners, and lines of symmetry. He tried to sketch one freehand in zero gravity, and it drifted off looking like a wobbly biscuit. Zara laughed.

Every regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles. This is a regular hexagon (6 of each).
▲
Triangle
3 sides · solar panel
■
Square
4 sides · floor tile
⬟
Pentagon
5 sides · control desk
⬢
Hexagon
6 sides · habitat module
More sides → the rounder the shape looks.
A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles. Look for its straight sides, corners, diagonals and axes of symmetry.
🚀 STEM Spark: Why space loves hexagons. Hexagons and triangles tessellate (fit together with no gaps) and spread force evenly, so they make structures that are strong and light, perfect for spacecraft.

Unit A: Polygons & Angles
LS 6.2.1
2

The Angle Detectives

🎨Measuring the hexagon module’s corner angles; a panel leaves a gap
images/c6_a2_angles.jpeg

To lock the hexagon habitat panels together, the angles had to be exact. Commander Dr. Farah called over comms: “Remember, engineers, the interior angles of any shape add up to (n − 2) × 180°, where n is the number of sides.”

A hexagon has n = 6 sides, so its angles add up to (6 − 2) × 180° = 4 × 180° = 720°. A regular hexagon shares that total equally between its 6 corners: 720° ÷ 6 = 120° at each corner. (A square has n = 4, so 360° in total, which is 90° at each corner.)

Interior angle = sum of interior angles ÷ number of sides. More sides → bigger corners.
🛠️ Ken’s Blooper: spot the mistake!
Ken rushed and set every hexagon corner to 90°, just like a square. The panels didn’t meet, so a gap opened and the air hissed out! 😲
“A hexagon isn’t a square, Ken. Each corner is 120°!” said Zara. They fixed it and the module sealed with a satisfying click.
Why did 90° leave a gap? What is 90° × 6, and what should it have been?
Interior angle of a regular polygon = sum of interior angles ÷ number of sides. The exterior angles of any polygon always add up to 360°.
🚀 STEM Spark: Angles keep you alive. In space, one wrong angle and the modules won’t seal. Engineers check every angle with a protractor and a computer before launch.

Unit B: Composite Shapes
CS 6.3 · LS 6.3.1 · 6.3.2
1

Two Shapes, One Module

🎨Zara & Ken join a square and a triangle into one solar array
images/c6_b1_module.jpeg

Time to build! Zara and Ken made each station part by joining two simple shapes into a composite shape. Their new solar array was a square with a triangle on top, a bit like a house.

Perimeter is the length all the way around the outside edge. Area is the space inside: area of a square = length × breadth, area of a triangle = ½ × base × height. For a composite shape, work out each part and add them.

Their array: square side 4 m → 4 × 4 = 16 m². Triangle base 4 m, height 3 m → ½ × 4 × 3 = 6 m². Total area = 16 + 6 = 22 m².

Composite area = triangle + square = 6 + 16 = 22 m²
🛠️ Ken’s Blooper: spot the mistake!
Adding up the perimeter, Ken also counted the hidden line where the two shapes join. His answer came out too big!
“Perimeter is only the outside edge, Ken. The join line is inside, so it doesn’t count,” said Zara.
Which edges belong to the perimeter of a composite shape: the outside ones, the inside join, or both?
Composite shape = two shapes joined. Area = add the parts. Perimeter = the outside edge only, never the hidden join.
🚀 STEM Spark: Build big from simple. Engineers make complicated parts by combining simple shapes. Area tells them exactly how much material (solar cells, panels, fabric) to pack for the mission.

Unit B: Composite Shapes
CS 6.4 · LS 6.4.1
2

Tanks and Blocks

🎨Filling the station’s water tank, made of a cuboid and a cube joined together
images/c6_b2_tanks.jpeg

The station needed a water tank. Ken built it from a cuboid and a cube joined together. Volume is the space inside a solid, and it tells you how much water fits.

A cube has all edges equal, so its volume = side × side × side. A cuboid can have different edges, so its volume = length × breadth × height. For a combined solid, find each volume and add them.

Big tank (cuboid): 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 m³. Small tank (cube): 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 m³. Total = 12 + 8 = 20 m³ of water. Dr. Farah smiled: “Enough for the whole crew!”

Combined volume = 12 m³ + 8 m³ = 20 m³ of water
Volume of a cube = side × side × side (all edges equal). Volume of a cuboid = length × breadth × height. Combined solid = add the volumes.
🚀 STEM Spark: Life-support maths. Volume tells engineers how much air, water and fuel a tank holds. In space, getting it right is the difference between a safe crew and a very thirsty one!

Unit C: Problem Solving
CS 6.5 · LS 6.5.1
1

The Moon Base Floor

🎨The crew tiles the L-shaped Moon-base floor, Earth in the black sky
images/c6_c1_moonfloor.jpeg

The squad landed on the Moon to build a base. First job: tile the habitat floor. The floor was an L-shape made of two rectangles. The mission budget was RM 8000, and each square metre of floor panel cost RM 200. Would there be enough?

Part A: 4 m × 3 m = 12 m². Part B: 6 m × 4 m = 24 m². Total floor = 12 + 24 = 36 m².

Total cost = 36 × RM 200 = RM 7200. That is less than RM 8000, so yes, they had enough! Ken wanted to tile the ceiling too, but Dr. Farah laughed: “One step at a time, engineer.”

Total floor = 12 + 24 = 36 m² · cost = 36 × RM 200 = RM 7200
To solve a space problem: ① find each area, ② add them for the total, ③ multiply by the cost, ④ compare to the budget.
🚀 STEM Spark: Plan before you pack. Engineers budget materials and money before launch. Running out of floor panels on the Moon is not an option: there is no shop up there!

LS 6.5.1
2

The Garden Module

🎨Growing Bornean greens in the garden module: a triangular bed + a rectangular walkway
images/c6_c2_garden.jpeg

To grow fresh food in orbit, the crew built a garden module. It had a triangular vegetable bed and a rectangular walkway beside it. To know how much soil and light were needed, they found the total area.

Triangular bed: base 6 m, height 4 m → ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 m². Rectangular walkway: 6 m × 2 m → 12 m². Total area = 12 + 12 = 24 m².

Soon, little green shoots of Bornean ulam were sprouting among the stars. 🌱

Plan view of the garden module, drawn to scale · total area = 12 + 12 = 24 m²
Break a tricky shape into a rectangle and a triangle, find each area, then add to get the total.
🚀 STEM Spark: Farming in space is real. Astronauts really do grow plants on space stations. Area maths tells them how much growing space and light each crop gets.

🔑 Answer Key

Check your work! Each block names the activity and the unit where you will find those questions.
✏️ Activity A: Polygon MissionUnit A: Polygons & Angles

1. 3 sides = triangle · 4 = square · 5 = pentagon · 6 = hexagon.

2. 6 straight sides, 6 corners, 6 axes of symmetry.

3. Square 90°; pentagon 108° (540 ÷ 5); hexagon 120° (720 ÷ 6).

4. (8 − 2) × 180° = 1080°.

5. 360° ÷ 6 = 60° at the centre.

6. Own design. Check all sides equal, all corners equal, and the angle matches the shape.

✏️ Activity B: Build It & Measure ItUnit B: Composite Shapes

1. A square and a triangle.

2. 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 30 cm (three square sides plus two slanted sides; the join is not counted).

3. 64 + 24 = 88 cm² (8 × 8, then ½ × 8 × 6).

4. 40 + 12 = 52 cm³.

5. 24 + 4 = 28 m³.

6. Own design. Area = square area + triangle area.

✏️ Activity C: Mission ProblemsUnit C: Problem Solving

1. 5 × 3 = 15 m².

2. ½ × 4 × 6 = 12 m².

3. 20 + 6 = 26 m².

4. 26 × RM 150 = RM 3900.

5. a. 12 + 30 = 42 m²   b. 42 × RM 200 = RM 8400   c. Yes (8400 is less than 9000).

6. 20 + 16 = 36 m² (½ × 8 × 5, then 8 × 2).

🛠️ Ken’s Blooper answers

Unit A (The Angle Detectives): 90° × 6 = 540°, but a hexagon’s interior angles must total 720°. Each corner should be 120°, so 90° is 30° too small at every corner and the panels leave a gap.

Unit B (Two Shapes, One Module): Only the outside edges belong to the perimeter. The hidden join between the two shapes is inside, so it is never counted.

🚀 For teachers and parents. “Own design” answers in Q6 have no single correct result. Look for correct method, labelled units (cm, m, m², m³, RM) and working that is shown step by step.
